A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same visible-thermal intrinsic decomposition work. Their complete main texts and supplementary materials, including equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison despite renaming and reorganization.

before.justification: V2 reports original decomposition experiments, simulated MIT evaluations, expert ordinality validation, loss/DDIP ablations, and low-light analysis.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and additionally reports spectral-reflectance analysis and evaluations before thermal equilibrium.

M1.justification: The ordinal constraints, losses, Double-DIP architecture, and optimization objective remain unchanged. Specifying three RGB channels and adding point-pair sampling details document the existing implementation without establishing a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: V3 adds validation using 427 USGS spectral materials under ASTM-G173 solar irradiance, a non-equilibrium thermal test scenario, and retexturing/relighting demonstrations in Figure 1. The existing VT-Intrinsic, color-chart, JoLHT-Video, and simulated MIT coverage remains; MIT evaluation moves into the supplement.

E2.justification: The simulated MIT quantitative comparison loses RGB-Retinex, Opt-LocalSmooth, IntrinsicDiffusion, RGB↔X, Intrinsic-v1, Intrinsic-v2, and CRefNet: v3 Table 2 reports only Ours. IntrinsicDiffusion remains in the MIT qualitative comparison. Comparator membership in the retained real-data benchmarks and supplementary gallery is unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols compare visible-only versus total absorbed-light ordinalities across all 90,951 material pairs and evaluate JoLHT-Video inputs at 10, 20, and 30 seconds against a 60-second reference. Existing decomposition metrics, acquisition procedures, and optimization iteration counts remain unchanged; added sampling and runtime specifics are disclosures.

E4.justification: V3 adds targeted checks of whether invisible spectral components reverse ordinalities and how decomposition tolerates non-equilibrium thermal conditions. Existing expert validation, loss/DDIP ablations, low-light analysis, and illustrated failure cases remain, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new spectral agreement percentage continues descriptive proportion reporting. Five parallel jobs are disclosed for runtime measurement, without establishing repeated-seed evaluation or a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds 94.2% spectral ordinality agreement and reports 72.3%, 79.0%, and 89.4% of steady-state performance at 10, 20, and 30 seconds. It removes the seven MIT baselines' numerical results and adds editing examples. Retained benchmark and ablation values are unchanged; MIT scores of 1.9% albedo and 0.5% shading equal v2's scaled values.

T1.justification: The image-formation and heat-transport derivations, Propositions 1–3, and supplementary proofs remain mathematically unchanged. The new transient discussion supplies a cited mechanism explanation and empirical evidence, without a new formal result or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: decomposition from one visible-thermal pair, ordinal self-supervision without learned priors, competitive reconstruction, and potential supervision for real-world datasets. Additional validation supports these existing claims; the VT-Intrinsic title prefix does not introduce a new contribution.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly excludes multiple colored illuminations and explains tolerance to small departures from thermal equilibrium through relative rather than absolute intensities. It discusses spectral violations near equal absorptances. The MIT results paragraph changes from claiming the lowest error over baselines to describing low average error.

D1.justification: New supplementary sections disclose point-pair sampling distances, angles, and mirrored boundaries, plus five-job runtime normalization on an RTX 4090. Runtime reporting becomes 48.22/5.63 seconds instead of approximately one minute/five seconds, without establishing a speedup. A project-page link is added; existing camera, preprocessing, and iteration details remain.

R1.justification: V3 adds the USGS Spectral Library Version 7 reference and expands positioning against JoLHT-Video by explicitly discussing radiometric calibration, active lighting control, and visible-only illumination requirements. The remaining related-work coverage is substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: expert validation moves from theory to experiments, qualitative evaluation precedes quantitative evaluation, and MIT evaluation and ablations move into a reorganized supplement. V3 also edits the introduction and related work, adds an introductory limitations summary, and updates the title and author header.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned with application panels, Figure 3's example montage is reduced and rearranged, and Table 1 loses its MIT columns and reorders the remaining groups. MIT results receive a separate supplementary table; the MIT visualization and ablation table move into the supplement while failure cases move into the main text. The final 15 supplementary pages are visually identical.

improvement.justification: The spectral and transient checks strengthen support for the physical assumptions, while clearer applicability limits and sampling/runtime disclosures improve assessability and reproducibility. Removing MIT baseline scores reduces comparative completeness, and the transient performance percentages lack a clear definition. Nevertheless, the retained real-data comparisons and ablations, together with the targeted validation and documentation gains, support a modest net improvement.
